query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix, whose overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation behavior across different temperatures remain unclear, what single intervention could improve its wear resistance under sliding conditions spanning different temperatures, friction velocities, and wear depths? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to the unchanged FeNiCrCoCu coating tested under identical conditions, defines the operating limits of the prediction, cites supporting evidence from the introduction, and proposes a falsification experiment capable of resolving microscopic deformation during wear.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of Titanium (Ti) into the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating to form a dual-phase (FCC + BCC) microstructure with nano-precipitates will significantly enhance wear resistance across a wide temperature range by promoting the formation of a stable, protective oxide layer and activating deformation twinning mechanisms that are suppressed in the single-phase FCC matrix.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix, characterized by a single-phase Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) structure with high stacking fault energy at elevated temperatures, leading to limited work hardening and potential softening during sliding wear.
generation.intervention: Alloying the FeNiCrCoCu coating with Titanium (Ti) to achieve a composition near FeNiCrCoCuTi0.5 (or similar stoichiometry) to induce phase separation into FCC and Body-Centered Cubic (BCC) phases and/or the formation of ordered L12 or B2 precipitates.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear conditions spanning temperatures from room temperature to elevated temperatures (e.g., 200°C–600°C), varying friction velocities, and varying wear depths in an atmospheric environment.
generation.structural_mediator: A dual-phase microstructure (FCC + BCC) containing nano-precipitates and a thermally stable, protective oxide layer (rich in TiO2/Cr2O3) formed on the wear track surface.
generation.mechanism: The addition of Ti stabilizes BCC phases and promotes the formation of ordered precipitates, which increases the lattice friction and hinders dislocation motion (solid solution strengthening). At elevated temperatures, the Ti-rich oxide layer forms a protective barrier that reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and lowers the coefficient of friction. Simultaneously, the reduced stacking fault energy in the modified matrix (due to Ti and Cr interactions) promotes deformation twinning and transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP), enhancing strain hardening and preventing catastrophic wear failure, unlike the single-phase FCC matrix which relies solely on dislocation glide.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ti-modified FeNiCrCoCu coating will exhibit a 30–50% reduction in wear rate and a 10–20% reduction in the coefficient of friction compared to the unmodified FeNiCrCoCu coating across the tested temperature range, with the wear mechanism shifting from adhesive/abrasive wear to mild oxidative wear.
generation.baseline: Unmodified FeNiCrCoCu coating tested under identical sliding conditions (temperature, velocity, depth) without Ti addition.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds for Ti contents between 0.1 and 0.5 atomic fractions; exceeding this range may lead to the formation of brittle complex intermetallic phases (as seen in AlCoCrFeNiTi systems with high Al/Ti), causing embrittlement and a sharp increase in wear rate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal Ti concentration for the FeNiCrCoCu system is unknown, as the provided evidence primarily discusses AlCoCrFeNiTi and CoNiCrFeMn systems. The interaction between Cu and Ti in this specific high-entropy matrix regarding phase stability and oxide formation kinetics is not explicitly detailed in the supplied records, introducing uncertainty in the precise phase fraction and oxide composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of coatings: (1) FeNiCrCoCu (baseline) and (2) FeNiCrCoCuTi0.5 (intervention). Subject both to reciprocating sliding wear tests at 25°C, 400°C, and 600°C with varying velocities. Perform post-wear analysis using Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) to observe dislocation structures and X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) to analyze the oxide layer composition.
measurements: Stacking Fault Energy (SFE) estimation via TEM diffraction contrast
Dislocation density and twin boundary density (TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the Ti-modified coating shows a higher wear rate than the baseline at any tested temperature, or if TEM analysis reveals no increase in deformation twinning or nano-precipitate density in the Ti-modified coating compared to the baseline, despite the presence of Ti.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy alloys based on 3d transition metals display rich and promising magnetic characteristics for various high-technology applications. Understanding their behavior at finite temperature is, however, limited by the incomplete experimental data for single-phase alloys. Here we use first-principles alloy theory to investigate the magnetic structure of polymorphic CoCrFeMnNi in the paramagnetic state by accounting for the longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) as a function of temperature. In both face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures, the LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr and Ni. The impact of LSFs is demonstrated on the phase stability, stacking fault energy and the fcc-hcp interfacial energy. The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc one at cryogenic temperatures, which results in negative stacking fault energy at these conditions. With increasing temperature, the stacking fault energy increases, suppressing the formation of stacking faults and nano-twins. Our predictions are consistent with recent experimental findings.

Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. High strength and ductility, often mutually exclusive properties of a structural material, are also responsible for damage tolerance. At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior. Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures.
